scenarios.title: The Service That Won't Start
scenarios.situation: A line-of-business app stops working on a Windows Server. You open Services (services.msc) and find its service in a Stopped state; its Startup Type is Automatic. A colleague says to just click Start and move on.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first response, and what do you check after?
choices: Start the service, then immediately check the Event Logs (System and Application) for the errors that stopped it — restarting without a cause lets it fail again.
Reinstall the application; a stopped service always means a corrupt install.
Set the startup type to Manual so it cannot crash again.
Reboot the server immediately without checking anything.
scenarios.why: Services with Automatic startup do not stop themselves — something told the service to stop. Event Viewer (System log for service-control events, Application log for the app's own errors) is the causal layer; services.msc is only the control layer. The professional habit is control first, cause second, fix third.
scenarios.hint: Which two windows show you what the service did (control) versus why it did it (cause)?
objectives: Windows core administration: services and event logs

scenarios.title: NTFS vs Share Permissions
scenarios.situation: A user complains they cannot write to a shared folder, though their manager swears 'everyone has full control on the share.' You inspect the folder and see NTFS permissions grant the user's group Read-only.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the user blocked, and what is the right fix?
choices: Windows applies the most restrictive of the combined share and NTFS permissions — NTFS Read-only wins. Grant Write in the NTFS permissions (following least privilege) rather than opening the share further.
Share permissions override NTFS, so the user should already have access — the problem must be the network.
Give the user Full Control at both layers to eliminate all future tickets.
Delete the share and recreate it; permissions do not survive a share rebuild.
scenarios.why: Effective access is the intersection of share and NTFS permissions: the most restrictive permission always wins. The modern best practice is to set the share to broad access (e.g., Authenticated Users: Full Control) and enforce the real policy at the NTFS layer, where permissions are granular, inheritable, and auditable.
scenarios.hint: When two layers both say something, which one wins — the generous one or the strict one?
objectives: Windows core administration: NTFS and sharing

scenarios.title: The Locked-Out Finance User
scenarios.situation: A finance user cannot log in and the help desk unlocked their account twice today. You check Active Directory Users and Computers and see the account is in the Finance OU, which has a Group Policy requiring a 15-character password, while the user keeps setting a 10-character one.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause and the proper resolution?
choices: A Group Policy on the Finance OU enforces 15-character passwords; the user's 10-character password fails policy, so logons fail. Reset the password to a policy-compliant value and explain the requirement.
The user is being hacked; disable the account immediately.
Move the user to a different OU to escape the policy.
Group Policy is broken and should be unlinked from the Finance OU.
scenarios.why: Group Policy applies by OU: policies linked to the Finance OU win for accounts in that OU (the LSDOU order — Local, Site, Domain, OU — means the closest link wins on conflict). The unlocks treated the symptom; the password-policy mismatch was the cause. The fix is a compliant password plus user education — not moving the user or breaking policy for one person.
scenarios.hint: If a setting lives on the OU and the user lives in the OU, where do you look first — the user or the policy?
objectives: Active Directory: OUs and Group Policy

scenarios.title: PowerShell: The Pipeline Fix
scenarios.situation: You need a list of all services currently running on a server whose names start with 'SQL', and you want just their names and statuses on screen. You know Get-Service lists services and Where-Object filters them.
choices: Get-Service | Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Running' -and $_.Name -like 'SQL*' } | Select-Object Name, Status
Get-Service -Name 'SQL*' | Where-Object Status = Running
Where-Object { Name -like 'SQL*' } | Get-Service -Running
Get-Service | Select-Object -First 10
scenarios.why: The pipeline passes objects, not text: Get-Service emits service objects, Where-Object filters on their Status and Name properties ($_.Status, $_.Name), and Select-Object projects just the properties you want. The -like operator with a wildcard handles the 'starts with SQL' match. Memorizing the cmdlet names matters less than the pattern: get → filter → shape.
scenarios.hint: What does the pipeline carry between commands — text lines or objects with properties?

scenarios.title: DNS: The Intranet Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that 'intranet' resolves to an old IP on some workstations but the correct new IP on others. The DNS zone on the Windows DNS server was updated an hour ago. You confirm the server returns the new address.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and how do you confirm it on a broken workstation?
choices: Stale resolver cache or an outdated DHCP-provided DNS configuration on the affected workstations. Run ipconfig /displaydns to inspect the cache and ipconfig /flushdns plus ipconfig /registerdns to refresh it.
The DNS server is lying; rebuild the zone from scratch.
The workstations need new network cards.
Block port 53 at the firewall to force a different resolution path.
scenarios.why: Windows caches DNS answers locally, and clients keep using the cache until its TTL expires — so a zone change propagates unevenly. ipconfig /displaydns shows the cached entry, /flushdns clears it, and /registerdns re-registers the client. When 'some machines work and some don't' after a DNS change, the cache is suspect number one.
scenarios.hint: If the server is right but the client is wrong, where between them can an old answer hide?

scenarios.title: Kerberos vs NTLM at 2 AM
scenarios.situation: After a domain migration, a legacy application authenticates users but its audit logs show NTLM authentication instead of Kerberos. The app runs on a server joined to the new domain, and users authenticate fine — but security policy requires Kerberos everywhere it is supported.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely reason the app fell back to NTLM?
choices: The application or its service principal name (SPN) is misconfigured — Kerberos needs a valid SPN for the service, and without one (or with a duplicate SPN), Windows silently falls back to NTLM. Check SPN registration with setspn -L and the event logs for Kerberos errors.
NTLM is stronger than Kerberos, so this is an improvement.
Kerberos requires the firewall to be disabled.
The domain controllers need to be rebooted nightly for Kerberos to work.
scenarios.why: Kerberos authentication requires the client to find a ticket for the exact service principal name; a missing or duplicated SPN breaks ticket issuance and Windows degrades to NTLM without telling the user. This is why legacy apps 'work but show NTLM' after migrations: the app was never registered properly in the new domain. setspn -L <account> lists registered SPNs; duplicates are a classic migration artifact.
scenarios.hint: Kerberos answers the question 'who vouches for this service?' What record provides that answer?
objectives: Active Directory: Kerberos and NTLM authentication

lessons.title: Windows Systems Administration — Core concepts
concepts: Core administration: services.msc controls service state and startup type; the Registry holds system configuration; Event Viewer (System, Application, Security logs) is the causal record — control first, cause second, fix third.
NTFS vs share permissions: effective access is the most restrictive of the two layers; enforce policy at the NTFS layer and keep shares simple.
Active Directory: forests contain trees of domains; OUs organize objects for Group Policy, which applies in LSDOU order (Local, Site, Domain, OU — closest link wins).
Authentication: Kerberos is the default domain protocol (ticket-based, needs correct SPNs); NTLM is the legacy fallback — its appearance in logs signals a misconfiguration to investigate.
PowerShell: the pipeline passes objects with properties — Get-VerbNoun cmdlets retrieve, Where-Object filters, Select-Object shapes output.
Windows networking: DNS resolves names (watch the client cache), DHCP assigns addresses and options; file/print services and Remote Desktop/Remote Access complete the server's network role set.

example.code:
# Audit: find every running service whose name starts with SQL,
# show name and status, export to CSV for the change ticket
Get-Service |
    Where-Object { $_.Status -eq 'Running' -and $_.Name -like 'SQL*' } |
    Select-Object Name, Status, StartType |
    Export-Csv C:\audit\sql-services.csv -NoTypeInformation
# Verify the file landed:
Get-Item C:\audit\sql-services.csv | Select-Object Length, LastWriteTime
example.walkthrough: This is the get → filter → shape pattern in one pipeline: Get-Service emits service objects, Where-Object keeps only running ones matching 'SQL*', Select-Object projects three properties, and Export-Csv persists the evidence. The final Get-Item confirms the artifact exists — the habit of verifying output is what separates a script from a hope.

pitfalls: Common trap: restarting a failed service without checking Event Viewer — you treated the symptom and the failure will recur.
Common trap: opening share permissions instead of fixing NTFS — the most restrictive layer wins, so broad shares plus tight NTFS is the correct posture.
Common trap: unlinking a Group Policy to fix one user's problem — policy is OU-scoped; fix the object or the setting, not the whole policy.
Common trap: treating NTLM in the logs as normal — its presence usually means Kerberos broke down (bad or duplicate SPN), and that deserves investigation.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Service Triage and NTFS Repair
labs.objective: Diagnose a stopped service via event logs and repair a file-share access problem at the NTFS layer.
steps: Open Services and identify the stopped line-of-business service; note its startup type.
Open Event Viewer and filter the System log for Service Control Manager events around the stop time.
Record the error and its likely cause in your notes before restarting anything.
Restart the service and confirm it stays running for two minutes.
For the share issue: inspect both the share permissions and the NTFS ACL on the folder.
Grant the user group Modify at the NTFS layer, leave the share at Authenticated Users: Full Control, and re-test access.

checks.hint: Use Get-WinEvent -LogName System and filter for the Service Control Manager source.
Run icacls on the folder to view or set the NTFS ACL granting Modify.

labs.title: AD OU Design and PowerShell Remoting
labs.objective: Create an OU structure, link a Group Policy correctly, and run a one-to-many PowerShell command across servers.
steps: In Active Directory Users and Computers, create an OU named Workstations-Finance under the domain root.
Link a password-policy GPO to the new OU and confirm it does not apply outside the OU.
Run gpresult /r on a test machine to verify the policy applies (LSDOU order).
Enable PowerShell remoting and open a session to a lab server with Enter-PSSession.
From your workstation, run Get-Service -Name Spooler -ComputerName SRV01,SRV02 to query both servers at once.
Write a Desired State Configuration concept note: what 'state' would you declare for the Spooler service, and why DSC declares outcomes instead of steps.

checks.hint: Run gpresult /r (or /h) to show which GPOs applied to the machine.
Type Enter-PSSession -ComputerName <server> to open the remote session.

behavioral.prompt: Walk me through how you troubleshoot a server that users say is 'down.'
behavioral.framework: Show a layered method: verify scope (one user vs all), check services, read event logs, test network, then communicate status.
points: Scope the blast radius first
Evidence before action (logs before reboots)
Keep users informed while you work
pitfalls: Rebooting as the first step
No communication plan

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you automated a repetitive task with PowerShell or scripting.
behavioral.framework: STAR: the repetitive task, the script or one-liner you wrote, the time saved, and how you made it safe (testing, -WhatIf).
points: Concrete before/after time savings
Testing approach before running against production
Sharing the script with the team
pitfalls: A script with no testing story
Automating something you did not fully understand

behavioral.prompt: How do you handle a change that could affect every user in the domain, like a Group Policy update?
behavioral.framework: Change control: test OU, pilot group, maintenance window, rollback plan, communication.
points: Never link untested policy at the domain level
Pilot on a representative OU first
Documented rollback
pitfalls: Deploying domain-wide on a Friday afternoon
No rollback plan

behavioral.prompt: A user with an urgent deadline asks you to 'just give me admin rights for today.' How do you respond?
behavioral.framework: Least privilege + alternatives: understand the actual need, offer a scoped solution (temporary group membership, run-as), follow approval process.
points: Empathy for the deadline without caving
A scoped alternative that solves the real problem
Follows the access-request process
pitfalls: Granting standing admin to be helpful
Refusing with no alternative offered

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to learn an unfamiliar Windows Server role or feature quickly.
behavioral.framework: STAR: the unfamiliar technology, how you learned it (docs, lab, testing), and how you proved it worked.
points: Lab-first approach before touching production
Official documentation as the source of truth
Validation step before declaring done
pitfalls: Learning directly on the production server
No verification of the result

behavioral.prompt: How do you document your administrative work so the next person can follow it?
behavioral.framework: Show the habit: change tickets, runbooks, scripts in version control, and notes that explain the why.
points: Documentation written for a stranger, not yourself
Why alongside the what
Kept where the team actually looks
pitfalls: Documentation that lives only in your head
Steps with no reasoning attached

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a disagreement with a colleague over how to configure something.
behavioral.framework: STAR: the technical disagreement, how you evaluated the options (docs, testing, risk), and how you reached a decision.
points: Evidence over ego — test or cite documentation
Respectful disagreement focused on the system
Team decision once made is supported
pitfalls: Winning the argument but damaging the relationship
Caving without evaluating the technical merit

behavioral.prompt: Where do you see your Windows administration skills going in the next two years?
behavioral.framework: Connect current skills to growth: automation depth, identity/hybrid, and security hardening.
points: Automation as a force multiplier (PowerShell, DSC concepts)
Identity as the security perimeter
Continuous learning habit
pitfalls: No direction at all
A plan that ignores security entirely

cheatsheet: services.msc: state (Running/Stopped) + startup type (Automatic/Manual/Disabled). Automatic services that stop did so for a reason — check logs.
Event Viewer: System (OS/service events), Application (app errors), Security (logons, audits). Filter by source and time.
NTFS vs share: effective access = most restrictive of both. Broad share + tight NTFS is the standard posture.
icacls: view and set NTFS ACLs from the command line.
AD: forest → trees → domains → OUs. GPOs apply in LSDOU order; closest link wins conflicts.
Kerberos = default domain auth (needs correct SPNs; setspn -L to inspect). NTLM in logs = investigate.
PowerShell pipeline: Get-* | Where-Object { $_.Prop -op value } | Select-Object Prop1, Prop2. Objects, not text.
Get-WinEvent -LogName System: modern event-log querying. gpresult /r: which GPOs applied.
DNS: ipconfig /displaydns, /flushdns, /registerdns. DHCP: scope, lease, reservations, options (DNS server, gateway).
Enter-PSSession / Invoke-Command: PowerShell remoting. DSC: declare desired state, the engine converges to it.

glossary.def: The top-level Active Directory container: one or more domain trees sharing a schema, configuration, and global catalog.
An AD partition with its own security boundary and authentication authority; users and computers join a domain.
A container inside a domain used to organize objects and scope Group Policy.
Centralized configuration management for AD-joined machines and users, applied in LSDOU order.
Local, Site, Domain, OU — the order Group Policy applies; the closest link wins on conflict.
The default Windows domain authentication protocol: ticket-based, requires correct service principal names.
Legacy Windows challenge-response authentication; its appearance in logs usually signals a Kerberos failure to investigate.
Service Principal Name: the identifier Kerberos uses to issue tickets for a service; missing or duplicate SPNs break Kerberos.
File-system-level access control on Windows volumes: granular, inheritable, and the correct enforcement layer.
Running commands on remote machines via Enter-PSSession (interactive) or Invoke-Command (one-to-many).
Desired State Configuration: declare the state a machine should be in; the engine converges the system to it.
Domain Name System: resolves names to IPs; Windows clients cache answers locally (ipconfig /displaydns).
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: assigns IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways, and DNS servers automatically.

simulations.title: Why Isn't the GPO Applying?
simulations.brief: A security baseline GPO applies to every OU except Finance. Diagnose the Group Policy failure.

steps.symptom: Baseline GPO linked at the domain level applies everywhere except the Finance OU.
evidence: Finance machines show the GPO as 'Denied (Security Filtering)'
The GPO's security filter lists only 'Workstation-Admins'
Finance machines are in 'Finance-Users' — nobody added them to the filter
options: Link the GPO directly to the Finance OU as well
Security filtering is the cause: the GPO only applies to principals in its filter — add 'Finance-Computers' (or Authenticated Users, per design) to the security filter instead of duplicating links
Run gpupdate /force on every Finance machine
steps.explain: 'Denied (Security Filtering)' names the mechanism: link order is fine, but the GPO's ACL doesn't include Finance's machines. Fix the filter once; duplicating links creates the OU-sprawl that causes the next mystery.

steps.symptom: Filter fixed, but one Finance laptop still doesn't apply the policy after gpupdate.
evidence: Event 1058: cannot access the SYSVOL share
Laptop is on the guest Wi-Fi, not the corporate LAN
Every wired Finance machine applied fine
options: The laptop can't reach SYSVOL from guest Wi-Fi — move it to the corporate network (or VPN) and gpupdate again; GPO needs the domain, not just the command
Disable the firewall on the laptop
steps.explain: gpupdate without domain connectivity is theater. Event 1058 says the client can't read SYSVOL — fix the network path (corporate LAN/VPN), then update. Always read the event log before rebuilding anything.

steps.symptom: All green. What permanent practice prevents the next GPO mystery?
evidence: Must catch filtering/link mistakes before users do
options: Email the team after every GPO change
A GPO change checklist: document link order, security filter, and WMI filters; verify with gpresult on a pilot machine in each affected OU before wide rollout
steps.explain: GPO changes get the same discipline as code: checklists, pilot OUs, gpresult verification. The checklist from this incident becomes the runbook for the next change.

simulations.debrief: Group Policy failures are almost always scope problems (links, filters, WMI) or connectivity (SYSVOL reachability). Read gpresult, read the event log, verify on pilots — in that order.

simulations.title: Patch Tuesday Triage
simulations.brief: It's Patch Tuesday. 400 servers, a critical RCE in the print spooler, and a maintenance window Friday. Run the triage.

steps.text: Critical RCE, print spooler, exploit chatter online. 400 servers across prod, staging, and lab. Maintenance window Friday 10 PM–2 AM. First move?

choices.label: Push the patch to all 400 servers immediately — critical means now
choices.feedback: Untested patches on 400 production servers is how you trade a vulnerability for an outage. Speed without staging is gambling.

choices.label: Risk-rank: patch internet-facing and print servers TODAY via emergency change; lab tonight; staging tomorrow; prod in Friday's window
choices.feedback: Blast-radius thinking: the exposed systems get the emergency change, everything else rides the normal ring progression. Risk reduced today, stability kept.

choices.label: Wait for Friday's window — process is process
choices.feedback: Process without judgment: the internet-facing print servers sit exploitable for 72 hours because the calendar said so.

steps.text: You pushed everywhere at once. 60 servers blue-screen on reboot — the patch conflicts with the EDR driver. 2 AM, phones ringing. What now?

choices.label: Keep pushing — the remaining 340 need the patch too
choices.feedback: Pushing through a known-bad interaction is how 60 becomes 400. Stop the line.

choices.label: Halt the rollout, roll back the 60 via the recovery image, open a P1 with the EDR vendor, and re-stage with the fixed driver combo
choices.feedback: Stop-the-line discipline: halt, recover, root-cause with the vendor, re-stage. The 340 wait — safely.

steps.text: Rings worked: lab clean, staging clean, Friday's prod window patched 380 servers with zero incidents. Monday's review: what becomes permanent policy?

choices.label: 'We got lucky — same process next month'
choices.feedback: It wasn't luck, it was rings. Failing to encode the win guarantees relearning it during the next critical RCE.

choices.label: Encode the ring model: emergency ring for exposed systems, lab→staging→prod progression, EDR-compat check as a mandatory gate, stop-the-line authority for the on-call
choices.feedback: The incident becomes infrastructure: rings, gates, and explicit stop authority. Next Patch Tuesday runs itself.

simulations.debrief: Patching is risk management, not speed: ring the rollout by exposure, gate on compatibility, and give the on-call stop-the-line authority. The policy is the product of the incident.

simulations.title: Join the Domain
simulations.brief: Order the steps to properly join a Windows machine to the domain and verify it.

steps.context: A new workstation needs to join the corp domain. Order the steps.
items: Verify network: the machine reaches a domain controller (DNS points at the DC)
Join the domain with a privileged account and reboot
Confirm the computer object appears in the correct OU (move it if needed)
Run gpupdate and verify with gpresult that baseline policies apply
Hand off: document the asset in inventory and notify the user

simulations.debrief: DNS first (domain join is DNS-dependent), join and reboot, OU placement (policies follow the OU), verify with gpresult, then document. Skip the verification and you'll meet the machine again — as a ticket.

simulations.title: Audit the Server Config
simulations.brief: A member server's hardening checklist has 3 failures. Find them.

steps.config:
# srv-hardening.conf — member server
admin_shares = enabled           # line 2
rdp_nla = required              # line 3
smb1 = enabled                  # line 4
local_admin = renamed           # line 5
firewall = on                   # line 6
llmnr = enabled                 # line 7
autoplay = disabled             # line 8

issues.description: Default administrative shares (C$, ADMIN$) enabled — lateral-movement fuel; rarely needed on member servers.
SMBv1 enabled — deprecated, unpatchable protocol and the WannaCry vector; no modern reason to run it.
issues.fix: smb1 = disabled; verify no legacy dependency first.

issues.description: LLMNR enabled — spoofable name resolution, the classic Responder attack surface.
issues.fix: llmnr = disabled via GPO; ensure DNS suffices.

simulations.debrief: Lines 3, 5, 6, 8 are hardened correctly (NLA, renamed admin, firewall on, autoplay off). The failures: admin shares, SMBv1, and LLMNR — the standard lateral-movement triad. Harden by default, exception by ticket.

simulations.title: Ransomware at 3 AM
simulations.brief: The on-call phone rings at 3 AM: file shares are encrypting, ransom notes appearing. Run the first hour.

steps.text: 3:07 AM. Reports: finance share encrypting, ransom notes in three directories, help desk phone lighting up. Your first three actions?

choices.label: Start investigating which variant it is — attribution guides response
choices.feedback: Attribution is hour-six work. Right now encryption is spreading per minute; every minute of analysis is terabytes lost.

choices.label: Isolate: kill the share server's network (keep it powered for forensics), disable the affected AD accounts, page the IR team and leadership
choices.feedback: Contain first: network-isolate the encrypting host, cut the compromised accounts' access, escalate. Analysis happens on a contained scene.

choices.label: Pay the ransom quickly — it's the fastest recovery
choices.feedback: Paying funds the next attack, doesn't guarantee decryption, and may be illegal depending on attribution. Never the first move.

steps.text: 4:30 AM. The encryption reached the backup server — it was domain-joined with the same credentials. What's the brutal lesson and the immediate move?

choices.label: Lesson: backups must be isolated (offline/air-gapped copies). Move: assess what's recoverable from the offline tapes and rebuild the domain from known-good media.
choices.feedback: The hard truth faced directly: domain-joined backups aren't backups. Recovery goes to the offline copies; the domain gets rebuilt, not cleaned.

choices.label: Try to decrypt with free tools while negotiating with the attackers
choices.feedback: Negotiation without contained scope or offline backups is surrender with extra steps.

steps.text: 5:00 AM. Spread contained to two servers. Forensics has memory captures. Leadership asks: 'Do we pay?' Your recommendation?

choices.label: 'Pay — it's faster than rebuilding.'
choices.feedback: Faster and wrong: no guarantee, funds crime, possible sanctions violation. Speed is not the criterion.

choices.label: 'No. We restore the two servers from last night's offline backups, rebuild credentials domain-wide, and publish the timeline. Paying is off the table.'
choices.feedback: The professional answer: offline backups make payment unnecessary, credential rebuild removes persistence, transparency preserves trust. This is what the 3 AM discipline bought.

simulations.debrief: Ransomware response is contain → escalate → recover from offline backups → rebuild trust. The 3 AM decisions are made by the runbook written at 3 PM: isolated backups, practiced isolation steps, and a no-payment policy decided in advance.

consoleSims.title: Work the Help Desk Queue
consoleSims.brief: Windows support lives in the queue. Log the ticket, assign it, and resolve it with the actual fix.

tasks.instruction: Create a P2 ticket titled 'GPO not applying on Finance laptops'.

params.title: GPO not applying on Finance laptops

tasks.hint: New ticket: TITLE exactly as given, PRIORITY P2.

tasks.instruction: Add a note to INC-9001: 'gpresult showed Denied (Security Filtering); filter corrected.'

params.text: gpresult showed Denied (Security Filtering); filter corrected.

tasks.hint: Add note: INC-9001 with the exact text.

tasks.instruction: Resolve INC-9001 with resolution 'Security filter fixed; gpupdate verified on pilot machines.'

params.resolution: Security filter fixed; gpupdate verified on pilot machines.

tasks.hint: Resolve form: INC-9001 with the exact resolution text.

consoleSims.debrief: Windows tickets close with evidence: what gpresult said, what was fixed, how it was verified. The note trail is the next admin's runbook.

consoleSims.title: Configure the Host Firewall
consoleSims.brief: Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security, simulated: allow RDP for admins only, block everything else by default.

tasks.instruction: Add a rule: INPUT chain, tcp port 3389, source 10.0.0.0/8, action ACCEPT — RDP for the admin network only.
tasks.hint: Rules: CHAIN INPUT, PROTOCOL tcp, PORT 3389, SOURCE 10.0.0.0/8, ACTION ACCEPT.

tasks.instruction: Add a rule: INPUT chain, tcp port 445, source 0.0.0.0/0, action DROP — no SMB from the internet, ever.
tasks.hint: Add rule: CHAIN INPUT, PROTOCOL tcp, PORT 445, SOURCE 0.0.0.0/0, ACTION DROP.

tasks.instruction: Set the INPUT chain default policy to DROP — the firewall denies what no rule allows.
tasks.hint: Default policies: CHAIN INPUT, POLICY DROP.

consoleSims.debrief: Host firewall discipline: RDP scoped to the admin network, SMB never from the internet, default-deny underneath. Every open port is a decision with a name on it.

consoleSims.title: Segment the Office Network
consoleSims.brief: The office switch needs VLANs: Finance isolated, printers separate, then save the config.

tasks.hint: In the Terminal section type: vlan 20 name FINANCE

tasks.instruction: Assign interface Gi0/5 to access VLAN 20 (the Finance printer port).
Set interface Gi0/24 to trunk mode (the uplink to the core).

consoleSims.debrief: Segmentation is policy in copper: Finance isolated at layer 2, uplinks trunked, config saved. Unsaved configs don't survive the next power outage.

consoleSims.title: Maintain the Asset Database
consoleSims.brief: The CMDB tracks every Windows asset. Create it, add the admin, grant access, back it up.

tasks.hint: Grants: DB assets, USER winadmin, PRIVILEGE SELECT.

consoleSims.debrief: You can't patch what you can't inventory: the asset database is the foundation of every Patch Tuesday, every audit, every incident response. Back it up like the domain depends on it.

terminalMissions.title: Survey the Server
terminalMissions.brief: Orient on the box: list the workspace and read the notes (your runbook shelf).
terminalMissions.success_message: Server surveyed. Read before you touch — the first rule of administration.

terminalMissions.title: Log the Change
terminalMissions.brief: Every change gets a log entry. Write the GPO change to change-log.txt.

checks.hint: Type: echo "GPO baseline: security filter fixed" > change-log.txt (no output on success).
Type: echo "verified: gpresult clean on 3 pilots" >> change-log.txt.

terminalMissions.success_message: Change logged. Undocumented changes are incidents waiting for a timestamp.

terminalMissions.title: Audit the Change Log
terminalMissions.brief: Count change entries and search for the verification marker.
terminalMissions.success_message: Log audited. Every change verified, every verification logged.

terminalMissions.title: Seal the Baseline
terminalMissions.brief: Hash the baseline version string — configuration drift detection starts here.

checks.hint: Type: sha256sum baseline-v42 finance-ou — the real hash plus your baseline are echoed.

terminalMissions.success_message: Baseline sealed. Drift is detected by comparing against the seal, not by memory.

terminalMissions.title: Check the Event Trail
terminalMissions.brief: Windows admins live in event logs. Read this log's edges and hunt errors.
terminalMissions.success_message: Event trail read. The log told you; you just had to ask.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the Environment
terminalMissions.brief: Confirm the administrative environment: identity and home.
terminalMissions.success_message: Environment verified. Know which context you're administering.

terminalMissions.title: Check Domain Reachability
terminalMissions.brief: A domain member that can't reach the DC is just a workgroup machine. Verify DNS and path.
terminalMissions.success_message: DC reachable. Domain join is DNS-dependent — verify the dependency.
